https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-ce.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will convene the country’s National Security Council on Tuesday over the migration crisis in Ceuta — 26 days after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco and overwhelmed local authorities. Sánchez held two online meetings with ministers on Aug. 7 and 17 to coordinate Spain’s response to the crisis in Ceuta. But this is the first time he’s called for an emergency meeting of his National Security Council, which includes part of his cabinet alongside defense and intelligence leaders. The meeting will begin at 8:30 a.m. in Madrid’s Moncloa Palace, El País reported . The prime minister had been under pressure to convene the body for weeks. Earlier this month, left-wing Izquierda Unida leader Antonio Maíllo called the meeting “essential” and urged Sánchez to rethink Spain’s relationship with Morocco. “First, holidays. Then, national security,” said Cuca Gamarra , a lawmaker for the center-right People’s Party, after Monday’s announcement. Advertisement Advertisement The Ceuta crisis erupted at the end of July, when tens of thousands of people entered the coastal semi-exclave in North Africa in the space of 24 hours, forcing Spain to deploy the army after border forces were overwhelmed. Sánchez flew to Ceuta and branded the crossings an “attack” and a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity. Most migrants subsequently returned to Morocco, but thousands remained. Madrid is now working to clear the remaining backlog. Around 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta on Aug. 13, the interior ministry said . The opposition People’s Party is demanding more immigration officers be sent to Ceuta to process returns around the clock, while the health ministry and regional governments are dispatching 25,000 vaccine doses to guard against outbreaks of infectious disease. The incident reignited a debate on unauthorized migration at the European level, with 22 EU leaders signing a letter calling for stronger EU external borders. It also triggered a feud between Spain and Italy after Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government imposed temporary checks on people arriving by air and sea from Spain, and Madrid retaliated with controls on travelers from Italy.

https://nineoclock.ro/felicia-alexandru-.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount British Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) announces the appointment of Felicia Alexandru as Executive Director. Effective August 17, 2026, Felicia will lead the Chamber’s executive operations. She will implement the strategic vision set by the Board of Directors and contribute to the development of initiatives dedicated to BRCC members and the Romanian-British business community. The appointment comes at a time of growing economic ties between the two countries. Bilateral trade in goods and services reached £10.4 billion in the four quarters ending March 2026, up 5.6% compared with the previous year, according to the latest data from the UK Department for Business and Trade. In her new role, Felicia Alexandru’s priorities will include strengthening dialogue between BRCC members, institutions and authorities; developing the Chamber’s events and initiatives programme; and facilitating new opportunities for collaboration, investment and commercial growth across the two markets, Romania and the UK. . “We are delighted to welcome Felicia at an important moment for the development of BRCC and the economic relationship between Romania and the United Kingdom. Her experience in diplomacy, consulting and leading complex teams will support the implementation of the strategic direction set by the Board of Directors. We aim for BRCC to become an increasingly relevant partner for its members, facilitate business connections that deliver tangible results, and contribute to turning bilateral potential into new investments and partnerships, ” said Robert Uzună, President of the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce . “I am taking on this role with great confidence, at an excellent time for our trade relations. I am joining BRCC’s talented team with a clear ambition to bring new momentum and to be close to every business leader. My priority is to listen to our members’ needs and turn the remarkable expertise within our network into real projects. Together with the Board of Directors, we will turn BRCC’s ambitious agenda into tangible results for the business community, through close dialogue with the authorities and active support for the expansion of Romanian and British companies across both markets,” said Felicia Alexandru, Executive Director of the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce. Experience in Diplomacy and Consulting Before joining BRCC, Felicia Alexandru led the Romanian operations of Aperio Intelligence, a British risk management and business intelligence consultancy. Prior to this role, beginning in 2021, she led the company’s due diligence teams in Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca. Between 2008 and 2019, Felicia worked at the British Embassy in Bucharest. Her professional experience also includes coordinating public integrity programmes in the non-governmental sector. Felicia Alexandru holds a degree in Political Science from the National University of Political Studies and Public Administration (SNSPA) in Bucharest and a master’s degree in International Relations and European Studies from Central European University in Hungary. Felicia Alexandru has also been actively involved in social-impact initiatives through volunteering focused on human rights, combating discrimination and climate change education. About the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce The British Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) is the leading organisation dedicated to promoting bilateral trade and investment between the United Kingdom and Romania. Through its mission to facilitate dialogue between companies and support the development of business relations, BRCC helps companies grow their operations and capitalize on opportunities in both markets. Founded in 1998, BRCC operates independently and has offices in London, Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca, leveraging an extensive network of corporate and individual members to create opportunities for growth and collaboration across the two countries. * This is partner content. https://www.dw.com/en/romania-prosecutor.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LC7z Romania has been investigating the Tate brothers for years [Sept 4, 2024] Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Prosecutors in Romania on Friday officially indicted social media influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan on trafficking charges, years after investigation into the brothers' activities began. Andrew Tate was indicted for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering. His brother has been indicted for complicity. The brothers hold dual US and British citizenship. They were arrested in Miami in late July, following a British request for their extradition on rape charges. Andrew Tate is one of the most prominent faces of the "manosphere" , a male-centered social media movement rooted in anti-feminist discourse. How misogynists take over social media To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did the Romanian prosecutors say about the Tates' indictment? The Tate brothers have been mainly based in Romania since 2017 , where they have been under criminal investigations since December 2022 on charges including human trafficking. Romanian prosecutors said the Tates recruited their victims by falsely claiming to be seeking a relationship or marriage. They would then force them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business from which they mostly kept the profit. The Romanian anti-organized crime prosecuting unit DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate's victims was only 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012, then moved her to Bucharest. He then went on to exercise physical violence and mental intimidation to force her to produce pornographic content for social media sites. Tristan was an accessory in the sexual exploitation committed by his brother, DIICOT said, using physical aggression to coerce the victim. According to prosecutors, the Tates kept $1.25 million (roughly €1 million) from the camshow income generated by sexually exploiting the victim, which amounts to some 80% of her gains. They then tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars. Misogyny on social media To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Can the Tates be extradited to Romania? The spokesperson for DIICOT said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek the brothers' extradition from the US. While they can be tried in absentia in Romania, the trial will not start immediately. Romanian laws stipulate that the indictment be sent to a preliminary court chamber for a judge to ensure the legality of the case files. The preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalize the report, as per the law, but indictments tend to take significantly longer. Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed misogynist , and his brother have denied any wrongdoing. "We ‌will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement. Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first. https://www.dw.com/en/why-many-syrians-f.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LPqN Despite terrible memories of death during the war, including that of her brother, Huda Khayti now often returns to her hometown of Douma Image: privat Advertisement Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad. Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria. Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center. "Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma." In Douma, Huda Khayti visits the grave of her murdered brother Image: privat Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia . Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere. Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity. "Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia." Justice served in Syria? The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice." Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too. In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings. Syria still scarred after 14-year civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just. But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process. Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors. Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies. In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime. Victim-centered process needed Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat , that burning in my eyes." For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained. Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition. For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice. "I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves." Huda Khayti also runs a women's center in Idlib and works with people in refugee camps on the Turkish border Image: privat At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past. " Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity." Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria. "So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning." The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information. The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime . It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State" . Return to Syria: Rebuilding and seeking justice in Yarmouk To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Investigating all war crimes "This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included." For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma. "It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained. Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected. It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said. In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice. "We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice." This article was originally written in German. At least 150 pro-LGBTQ protesters detained in Istanbul crackdown Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 15/09/2026 - 18:05 GMT+2 Turkish police detained at least 150 pro-LGBTQ protesters in Istanbul on Tuesday, 15 September, during a demonstration against a nationwide crackdown on the LGBTQ community. … More Protesters gathered outside the Çağlayan courthouse, chanting for the release of people detained in recent raids. Police surrounded the group and warned that the demonstration was unauthorised before moving in and taking protesters away in police buses. Two journalists were among those detained. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The protest followed operations carried out across Turkey on 12 and 13 September under the name “My Family Is Safe” . Feminist activist Feride Eralp said 162 people had been taken into custody nationwide, with more than 20 arrested and more than 30 detained in Istanbul. She also said six LGBTQ associations in the city had been raided. The operations have been linked by the government to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s “Decade of the Family and Population” initiative. Same-sex relations are not illegal in Turkey, but LGBTQ people have faced increasing pressure from the authorities in recent years. The European Union expressed concern over the arrests on Monday and urged Ankara to respect human rights. https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: One of the ships stranded in the Strait of Hormuz. Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island Wed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 01.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance. In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz. View image in fullscreen Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters View image in fullscreen He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home. Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different. Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation. View image in fullscreen One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped. According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired. Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel . With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes. But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan. View image in fullscreen Fishers returning from sea View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety. View image in fullscreen Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult. “Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks. View image in fullscreen Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas “This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk. Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night. View image in fullscreen Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”. View image in fullscreen Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer View image in fullscreen A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds. The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army. View image in fullscreen Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war “The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted. View image in fullscreen The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman. Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island. View image in fullscreen One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war. View image in fullscreen Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter “Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.” Explore more on these topics The Guardian picture essay Iran Strait of Hormuz Middle East and north Africa features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
